title: The Sarpanch Reaches 100: Shreyas Iyer Joins IPL's Most Elite Captains' Club
excerpt: Punjab Kings skipper becomes only the fifth captain to reach 100 IPL matches, matching Dhoni's win rate and standing alone as the only leader to guide three franchises to finals
body:
The 'Sarpanch' of the IPL has added another line to his growing legend. When Shreyas Iyer walked out to lead Punjab Kings against Royal Challengers Bengaluru at Dharamsala's HPCA Stadium on May 17, he became only the fifth captain in Indian Premier League history to reach 100 matches as skipper — joining an elite fraternity that includes MS Dhoni, Rohit Sharma, Virat Kohli, and Gautam Gambhir.

## A Win Rate That Speaks Volumes

The milestone is more than ceremonial. Across his 100 matches at the helm, Iyer boasts a 58.3 per cent win rate — a figure that matches Dhoni's all-time best and places him among the most effective leaders the tournament has ever seen. He has accumulated 56 wins as captain, an achievement that looks even more striking when measured against the context in which they were earned.

https://www.instagram.com/shreyasiyer96/

What separates Iyer from every other captain in IPL history, however, is something no statistical model can fully capture: versatility under pressure. He is the only skipper ever to have led three different franchises to IPL finals. He guided Delhi Capitals to the final in 2020, masterminded Kolkata Knight Riders' title charge, and then steered Punjab Kings to their first-ever final in 2025 — a feat that seemed unthinkable for a franchise long synonymous with underachievement.

## From Mumbai Prodigy to Franchise Transformer

Born in Mumbai and a product of the city's fiercely competitive domestic cricket circuit, Iyer's rise was never conventional. He first took charge of Delhi Capitals as a relatively untested 24-year-old, transforming a perennial bottom-dweller into serious contenders. His move to KKR saw him deliver an IPL trophy, and his current stint at PBKS has given the franchise its most competitive era.

This season has tested that reputation, though. Punjab entered the RCB clash on the back of a five-game losing streak, their early-season dominance a fading memory. The team that once sat atop the points table now finds itself scrambling for a playoff berth, needing results to go their way in the tournament's final stretch.

Iyer himself has led from the front with 396 runs at an average of 49.50 this season, shouldering the burden with both bat and tactical acumen.

## The Bigger Picture for NRI Cricket Fans

For the millions of cricket-mad Indians watching from living rooms in New Jersey, living rooms in London, and sports bars in Toronto, Iyer's milestone carries a particular resonance. The IPL has become the primary connective tissue between the diaspora and Indian cricket culture — a shared language that bridges time zones and continents.

Iyer's journey from a confident young Mumbaikar to one of the most successful captains in T20 franchise history mirrors a broader shift in Indian cricket. The old guard — Dhoni, Kohli, Rohit — are in the twilight of their IPL careers. Iyer, at 31, represents the bridge generation: tested enough to command respect, young enough to shape the tournament's next chapter.

The match itself carried additional stakes beyond Iyer's personal landmark. RCB, the defending champions, were without regular captain Rajat Patidar, who was ruled out with concussion symptoms from a bouncer in a previous fixture. Jitesh Sharma stepped in to lead Bengaluru, adding another layer of intrigue to a contest where both teams' playoff destinies hung in the balance.

## What Lies Ahead

With the league stage entering its final week before the May 31 final in Ahmedabad, Punjab Kings' season hinges on the remaining matches. For Iyer, however, the 100-match milestone is less a capstone than a checkpoint. At his current trajectory, he could well end up as the most-capped captain in IPL history — a distinction that would place him alongside Dhoni in the pantheon of T20 leadership.

For diaspora fans who have watched the IPL evolve from a flashy experiment into a global sporting institution, Iyer's quiet, sustained excellence as a captain offers something increasingly rare in modern cricket: patience rewarded, consistency celebrated, and leadership valued beyond mere star power.
